facts.query: How tall are the Great Pyramid and other famous monuments?
facts.explanation: The Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for thousands of years. Roman builders achieved remarkable heights with concrete and arches, and medieval cathedrals finally overtook the pyramid. The Eiffel Tower, built of iron, more than doubled them all.

facts.query: When were the big breakthroughs in communication?
facts.explanation: For most of history, messages moved only as fast as a person could carry them. Paper and printing made writing cheap to copy, the telegraph made messages travel by wire, and radio, television and the internet followed in a rapid burst.

facts.description: Cai Lun, an official of the Han court, is credited with presenting a method of making paper.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica: paper, history

facts.label: Movable type in China
facts.description: Bi Sheng invents movable type made of baked clay, sometime between 1041 and 1048.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Bi Sheng; printing, history

facts.label: Gutenberg Bible printed
facts.description: Johannes Gutenberg's press in Mainz completes the Gutenberg Bible, around 1455.
facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gutenberg Bible

facts.description: Johann Carolus publishes the Relation in Strasbourg, widely recognised as the first newspaper.
facts.sourceNote: World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA)

facts.label: Telephone patented

facts.label: Radio signal crosses the Atlantic

facts.sourceNote: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Guglielmo Marconi

facts.query: If all of human history were squeezed into one day, when did things happen?
facts.explanation: Our species has existed for a very long time, but almost everything we think of as history happened at the very end. Squeeze it all into a single day and farming arrives in the last hour, writing in the last minutes, and the modern world in the final seconds.

facts.label: Earliest known Homo sapiens
facts.description: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, are the oldest known remains of our species, about 300,000 years old.

facts.query: How did the ancient Egyptians make mummies?
facts.explanation: Egyptians believed the body had to be preserved for the soul to live on in the afterlife. Embalmers removed the parts that would decay first, dried the body with natron salt, then wrapped it carefully in linen. Priests performed rituals at every stage.

facts.label: Purify the body
facts.title: Purify the body
facts.description: The body is washed with palm wine and rinsed with water from the Nile.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Remove the brain
facts.title: Remove the brain
facts.description: A long hook is pushed through the nose to break up and draw out the brain, which was thought to be unimportant.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Remove the organs
facts.title: Remove the organs
facts.description: A cut in the left side lets embalmers take out the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines. The heart is left in place.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Store the organs
facts.title: Store the organs
facts.description: The organs are dried and placed in canopic jars, each guarded by one of the four sons of Horus.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Dry the body
facts.title: Dry the body
facts.description: The body is packed and covered with natron salt for about 40 days until all moisture is gone.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Stuff and anoint
facts.title: Stuff and anoint
facts.description: The dried body is filled with linen and sawdust and rubbed with oils and resins to keep the skin supple.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Wrap in linen
facts.title: Wrap in linen
facts.description: Hundreds of metres of linen strips are wound around the body, with protective amulets tucked between layers.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies

facts.label: Opening of the Mouth and burial
facts.title: Burial
facts.description: Priests perform the Opening of the Mouth ritual, and the mummy is placed in its coffin and tomb.
facts.sourceNote: British Museum; Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History: Egyptian mummies
